card:
Give it a few years and TVs will be free, but....

You'll just have to sit through a 2-minute ad before switching channels, pay $9.99 a month to turn up the volume, and upgrade to Premium if you want to use the remote.
caption:
The TV is cheap now because YOU are the product.

That's not a joke anymore. It's the business model.

Smart TVs often sell close to cost because the money comes later:
• Ads built right into the home screen
• Viewing data sold to advertisers
• Streaming apps that each want a monthly fee

The sticker price was never the real price.

What nobody tells you: the "cheap" setup can quietly cost more than cable ever did once every subscription stacks up.

A few ways to push back:
1. List every streaming charge on the card statement this month
2. Keep one or two, rotate the rest month to month
3. Turn off "viewing data" or ACR in the TV's privacy settings
4. Check what the local library streams for free

The goal isn't zero fun. It's paying for what actually gets watched.

How many streaming services are on the card right now?

#JustMoney #Subscriptions #MoneyTips

card:
TURN 12 PTO DAYS INTO 42 DAYS OFF IN 2027

• Jan 1-4 (4 days): 1 PTO
• Jan 15-18 (4 days): 1 PTO
• Feb 12-15 (4 days): 1 PTO
• May 28-31 (4 days): 1 PTO
• Jun 18-21 (4 days): 1 PTO
• Jul 2-5 (4 days): 1 PTO
• Sep 3-6 (4 days): 1 PTO
• Nov 25-28 (4 days): 1 PTO
• Dec 23-27 (5 days): 2 PTO
• Dec 30-Jan 3 (5 days): 2 PTO

Save this before the whole office requests these dates.
caption:
12 PTO days. 42 days off. Same calendar everyone else gets.

The trick is simple: put PTO right next to holidays and weekends.

Every Friday or Monday next to a holiday turns 1 PTO day into a 4-day weekend. When a holiday lands on a Thursday or a weekend, 2 PTO days can turn into 5 days off.

What nobody tells you: the best dates go first. Whoever requests early usually wins.

How to make this work:
1. Check which holidays the company actually observes (Juneteenth, MLK Day and Presidents Day aren't universal)
2. Request the December dates now, those disappear fast
3. Book travel early, flights around long weekends climb quickly
4. Use the rest of the PTO for one real week away

Unused PTO is part of the pay package left on the table. Use it.

Which long weekend is getting booked first?

#JustMoney #PTO #WorkLifeBalance

card:
It's OK to rewear the same jacket.

It's OK to keep your iPhone 13.

It's OK to buy a used couch off Facebook Marketplace.

It's OK to live in a 1,900 square foot house.

A simple life is not a failure.

Too many people are going broke trying to look rich.
caption:
Looking rich and being rich are two completely different budgets.

One shows up on Instagram. The other shows up in a savings account.

A new phone every year. A leased SUV. A house sized for guests who visit twice a year. Each one feels small. Together they eat the paycheck.

What nobody tells you: most people who are actually doing well look pretty boring from the outside.

A few "boring" moves that add up:
• Keep the phone until it stops working, not until a new one drops
• Buy furniture used, a solid couch lasts decades
• Buy the house that fits the life, not the one that impresses people
• Rewear clothes without apologizing for it

Every dollar that doesn't go to looking successful can go to being comfortable.

What's one thing that got easier to skip once the pressure to impress was gone?

#JustMoney #FrugalLiving #PersonalFinance

card:
The average new car payment just hit $787 a month.

Over 1 in 4 new car loans now stretch 84 months or longer.

That's not a car. That's a 7-year subscription to something that loses value every day.
caption:
$787 a month. For 7 years. On something that's worth less every single day.

That's where new car buyers are right now, according to Edmunds data.

The average amount financed on a new car is over $44,000. More than a quarter of new car loans now run 84 months or longer. The average buyer pays close to $10,000 in interest over the life of the loan.

What nobody tells you: on a 7-year loan, most people owe more than the car is worth for years. Then they trade it in and roll that debt into the next car.

Before signing for a new car:
1. Look at the total price, not the monthly payment
2. Keep the loan at 60 months or less if possible
3. Get pre-approved at a credit union before the dealership
4. Price a 2 to 3 year old used version of the same model

A car is transportation. It shouldn't be a second rent payment.

What's the longest car loan anyone in the family has signed?

#JustMoney #CarLoans #DebtFree

card:
A $5,000 credit card balance at 20% APR, paying only the minimum:

About 23 years to pay it off.
About $7,700 in interest.

The minimum payment is designed to keep you paying, not to set you free.
caption:
$5,000 on a credit card can turn into almost $13,000 paid back. Here's how.

Credit cards average close to 20% APR right now.

Pay only the minimum on a $5,000 balance and it takes about 23 years to clear, with roughly $7,700 in interest on top (based on Bankrate's calculator).

What nobody tells you: the minimum is mostly interest. The balance barely moves for the first few years.

How to get out faster:
1. Pay a fixed amount every month, not the minimum, even $50 more helps
2. Attack the highest APR card first
3. Call the card company and ask for a lower rate, it costs nothing to ask
4. Look at a 0% balance transfer card if the credit score allows it, and read the transfer fee
5. Stop adding new charges while paying it down

Interest is the price of waiting. The sooner it's gone, the cheaper it is.

What's the APR on the card in the wallet right now?

#JustMoney #CreditCardDebt #DebtFree

card:
Skipping the full 401(k) match is turning down a raise.

Company matches 50% up to 6%? On a $60,000 salary, that's $1,800 a year of FREE money left on the table.
caption:
There's a raise sitting in a lot of benefits portals that nobody clicks on.

It's called the 401(k) match.

Here's the math on a common match of 50% up to 6%:
• Salary: $60,000
• Put in 6%: $3,600 a year
• Company adds 50% of that: $1,800 a year

That $1,800 is part of the pay package. Skipping it is like telling payroll to keep it.

What nobody tells you: many plans have a vesting schedule, so the match may only fully belong to the employee after a few years. Still worth getting.

How to grab it:
1. Log into the benefits portal and find the match formula
2. Set the contribution to at least the match percentage
3. Pick a low-cost target date or index fund if unsure
4. Bump it up 1% every time a raise hits

Free money is rare. This is one of the few places it actually exists.

Does the company match, and what's the formula?

#JustMoney #401k #Retirement

card:
Unpopular opinion: An emergency fund is not "lazy money."

It's the reason a $1,200 car repair is an inconvenience instead of a credit card bill at 20%.
caption:
People love to say cash is "doing nothing." Cash is doing a very important job.

It's keeping emergencies from becoming debt.

Without savings, a $1,200 transmission repair goes on a credit card at around 20% APR. Paid off slowly, that one bad week can cost hundreds extra.

With savings, it's just an annoying Tuesday.

What nobody tells you: the emergency fund isn't supposed to grow fast. It's supposed to be there.

Building one without it feeling impossible:
1. Start with a first goal of $1,000
2. Then work up to 3 to 6 months of basic expenses
3. Keep it in a high-yield savings account, separate from checking
4. Automate a small transfer every payday
5. Refill it right after using it

Investing is for the future. The emergency fund is for right now.

How many months of expenses would feel "safe" to have saved?

#JustMoney #EmergencyFund #Savings

card:
Inflation is back up to 3.7%.

If this year's raise was 2%, that's not a raise. That's a pay cut with a nicer email.
caption:
A 2% raise in a 3.7% inflation year means the paycheck buys LESS than last year.

US consumer prices rose 3.7% over the 12 months ending September, according to the Labor Department.

So a raise has to beat that number just to stay even.

What nobody tells you: "cost of living adjustment" and "raise" aren't the same thing. Keeping up with prices isn't getting ahead.

What to do about it:
1. Do the math before the review: last raise vs inflation
2. Pull up market pay data for the role (job boards and salary sites help)
3. Write down 3 concrete wins from this year with numbers
4. Ask for a specific number, not "whatever is fair"
5. If the answer is no, ask what it would take, in writing

Sometimes the biggest raise comes from a new offer. That's not disloyal, it's math.

Did this year's raise beat inflation?

#JustMoney #Inflation #SalaryNegotiation

card:
Mortgage rates are back above 7%.

$400,000 loan at 7.3%: about $2,740 a month.
$400,000 loan at 3%: about $1,690 a month.

Same house. Over $1,000 a month more. Before taxes and insurance.
caption:
Same house. Same loan. Over $1,000 a month difference, just from the rate.

Freddie Mac's weekly average for a 30-year fixed mortgage was 7.32% in late October.

On a $400,000 loan, principal and interest alone:
• At 7.3%: about $2,740 a month
• At 3%: about $1,690 a month

That's over $12,000 a year more for the exact same home. And property taxes and insurance come on top.

What nobody tells you: the rate matters as much as the price. A small rate difference can beat a big discount on the house.

If buying is on the table:
1. Get quotes from at least 3 lenders on the same day
2. Ask what paying points would cost vs save
3. Run the payment at today's rate, not a hoped-for future rate
4. Keep the total housing cost under about 30% of take-home pay

Refinancing later is possible, but it's never a guarantee.

Is buying a home on the plan for the next 2 years?

#JustMoney #MortgageRates #HomeBuying

card:
Streaming, cloud storage, the gym nobody goes to, the app everyone forgot about.

$15 here. $12 there.

It's never one big expense. It's 14 small ones.
caption:
Nobody goes broke from one $12 charge. It's the 14 of them.

Subscriptions are built to be forgettable. Small price, auto-renew, no reminder.

Add up streaming, music, cloud storage, a gym membership, delivery passes, apps and "free trials" that weren't cancelled, and it can easily pass $200 a month.

That's $2,400 a year that never feels like spending.

What nobody tells you: companies count on people not checking. A forgotten subscription is pure profit for them.

A 15-minute cleanup:
1. Open the last 2 months of bank and card statements
2. Highlight every recurring charge
3. Cancel anything not used in the last 30 days
4. Set a calendar reminder for every free trial the day it starts
5. Rotate streaming services instead of keeping all of them

Keep what's actually loved. Cut what's just habit.

What subscription is everyone paying for but barely using?

#JustMoney #Subscriptions #Budgeting

card:
Invest $300 a month from 25 to 65 at a 7% average return: about $787,000.

Start at 35 instead: about $366,000.

Waiting 10 years cost over $420,000. The extra contributions would have been $36,000.
caption:
Ten years of waiting can cost more than ten years of working.

Here's the math at a 7% average yearly return, $300 a month:
• Start at 25, invest until 65: about $787,000
• Start at 35, invest until 65: about $366,000

The person who started early only put in $36,000 more. The difference at the end is over $420,000.

That's compound growth. Early dollars have more time to grow, and then their growth grows too.

What nobody tells you: returns aren't guaranteed and markets go down sometimes. But time in the market is the one thing nobody can buy back later.

How to start small:
1. Open a Roth IRA or use the work 401(k)
2. Pick a low-cost broad index fund or target date fund
3. Automate the same amount every month
4. Don't panic sell when the market drops

$300 not possible yet? Start with $50. Starting matters more than the amount.

At what age did investing start for most people here?

#JustMoney #Investing #CompoundInterest

card:
Get a $10k raise.
Upgrade the apartment, the car, the phone, the takeout.

A year later, still living paycheck to paycheck.

Just a more expensive version of it.
caption:
More money doesn't fix the paycheck-to-paycheck problem on its own.

It's called lifestyle creep. Income goes up, spending quietly goes up right behind it.

A $10,000 raise is usually closer to $7,000 to $8,000 after taxes. A nicer apartment and a newer car payment can swallow that in a few months.

What nobody tells you: the upgrades become the new normal fast. Then they're hard to undo.

How to let a raise actually change things:
1. Decide where the raise goes BEFORE the first bigger paycheck lands
2. Try a 50/50 split: half to savings or debt, half to enjoying life
3. Bump the 401(k) contribution the same week the raise starts
4. Wait 3 months before any big upgrade
5. Track net worth, not just income

A raise should buy freedom, not just fancier bills.

What's the first thing that usually gets upgraded after a raise?

#JustMoney #LifestyleCreep #Budgeting

card:
Buy now, pay later is just a credit card wearing a hoodie.

Four easy payments on sneakers, a couch, concert tickets, and dinner, all at the same time, is how people go broke "interest free."
caption:
"Just 4 easy payments" is easy exactly once. Then it's 4 payments on 6 different things.

Buy now, pay later apps make every purchase feel small. That's the point.

One plan is fine. The trouble starts when several plans overlap and the payments hit the same week as rent.

What nobody tells you: missed payments can mean late fees, and some providers now report to credit bureaus. Some longer plans also charge interest.

Keep BNPL from running the budget:
1. Only use it for things that would be bought in cash anyway
2. Keep it to one active plan at a time
3. Put every due date in the calendar
4. Never use it for food or everyday spending
5. Check the app for every open plan right now and total them

If it can't be paid for in full today, it might not fit the budget today.

How many BNPL plans are open right now, honestly?

#JustMoney #BuyNowPayLater #MoneyTips

card:
Rich is a $90,000 truck in the driveway.

Wealthy is $90,000 sitting in an index fund that nobody knows about.
caption:
The neighbor with the nicest truck might have the smallest savings on the block.

Rich is what people can see. Wealthy is what keeps growing when nobody's looking.

A $90,000 vehicle loses a big chunk of its value in the first few years. $90,000 in a broad index fund has historically grown over long periods, though never in a straight line.

What nobody tells you: real wealth is usually invisible. No logo, no badge on the grille.

Building the quiet kind:
• Pay attention to net worth, not stuff
• Drive a reliable car longer than feels exciting
• Invest automatically before spending
• Avoid debt on things that lose value
• Let the money grow without announcing it

Nobody's impressed by an index fund at a barbecue. That's fine. It's not for them.

What would $90,000 invested change in the next 10 years?

#JustMoney #Wealth #Investing

card:
It's not a deal if it wasn't on the list.

Saving 40% on something nobody needed is still spending 60%.
caption:
Black Friday is great at one thing: making spending feel like saving.

"40% off" sounds like money back in the pocket. It isn't. It's still 60% of the price going out the door.

What nobody tells you: plenty of "sale" prices show up again in other months. Countdown timers and "only 3 left" banners are designed to rush the decision.

A simple Black Friday game plan:
1. Make the list BEFORE looking at any ads
2. Set a total budget and stick to it
3. Check price history before buying big items
4. Leave items in the cart for 24 hours
5. Unsubscribe from store emails the week after

A real deal is something already planned, at a lower price. Everything else is just shopping.

What's actually on the list this year?

#JustMoney #BlackFriday #SmartSpending

card:
Ask for a raise: "We can do 3%."

Get an offer somewhere else: suddenly there's budget for 12%.

Loyalty is great. It just doesn't pay rent.
caption:
Funny how the budget appears the moment someone has another offer.

It happens all the time. Raises for people who stay are often modest. Bigger jumps tend to come with a new job or a counteroffer.

What nobody tells you: companies set raise budgets in advance. A counteroffer comes from a different bucket, the "it costs more to replace them" bucket.

How to get paid what the role is worth:
1. Know the market rate for the job title and city
2. Keep a running list of wins with real numbers
3. Ask for a specific number at review time
4. Interview elsewhere every year or two, even just to stay informed
5. If a counteroffer comes, ask why it wasn't offered before

Staying at a great company is a fine choice. Just make it a choice, not a default.

Has a new job ever paid way more than a raise would have?

#JustMoney #SalaryNegotiation #CareerGrowth

card:
Pay $600 a month for health insurance.
Get sick.
Pay the $5,000 deductible.
Then pay 20% of whatever's left.

Somehow that's called the "good" plan.
caption:
Insurance isn't "covered." It's covered AFTER the deductible, and then mostly covered.

Here's how a lot of plans actually work:
• Premium: paid every month, sick or not
• Deductible: paid fully before the plan helps much
• Coinsurance: a share of the bill (often 20%) after that
• Out-of-pocket max: the most paid in a year for covered care

What nobody tells you: the out-of-pocket max is the number to plan around. That's the real worst case.

How to protect the budget:
1. Find the plan's out-of-pocket maximum and write it down
2. Build savings toward that number
3. If on a high-deductible plan, use an HSA, it's triple tax advantaged
4. Always ask for an itemized bill and check for errors
5. Ask about payment plans and financial assistance before paying

Healthcare costs are confusing on purpose. Knowing the numbers is the only defense.

Does anyone actually know their out-of-pocket max?

#JustMoney #HealthInsurance #MoneyTips

card:
Tip screens at the coffee counter.
Tip screens at self-checkout.
Tip screens for a bottle of water handed across the counter.

18%, 20%, 25% for turning an iPad around.
caption:
The iPad flips around and suddenly it's a decision about character.

Tip prompts are everywhere now. Coffee, bakeries, kiosks, even some self-checkout lanes.

What nobody tells you: those screens are designed so the "no tip" option is small and awkward. The default buttons often start at 18% or higher.

Tipping is personal, and service workers depend on it in a lot of jobs. But it helps to have a plan instead of reacting to a screen.

A simple approach:
• Tip as usual for sit-down service, delivery and personal services
• Decide in advance what feels right for counter service
• "Custom" is always an option
• Notice how much tipping adds up in a month

There's no wrong answer, just a budget that deserves to be intentional.

Where's the strangest place a tip screen has shown up?

#JustMoney #Tipping #Budgeting

card:
$150 used to be a full cart.

Now it's two bags, no snacks, and a long look at the receipt in the parking lot.
caption:
Everyone's done the parking lot receipt stare. It's not just in people's heads.

Food prices have climbed a lot over the past several years, and the weekly grocery run shows it more than almost anything.

What nobody tells you: store brands are often made in similar factories as name brands, and the price gap can be 20% to 30%.

A few ways to stretch the grocery budget:
1. Plan meals around what's on sale, not the other way around
2. Buy store brand for staples like rice, beans, flour and frozen veggies
3. Check the unit price on the shelf tag
4. Shop with a list and eat before going
5. Use the freezer, leftovers and bulk buys save real money

Small swaps every week add up to hundreds a year.

What's one item that got way more expensive lately?

#JustMoney #GroceryBudget #Inflation

card:
$7,500 a year into a Roth IRA from 25 to 65, at a 7% average return:

About $1.5 million.
Total put in: $300,000.

And the growth comes out TAX FREE in retirement.
caption:
$300,000 in. About $1.5 million out. And no tax on the way out.

That's the power of a Roth IRA over a long time.

The IRA contribution limit for 2026 is $7,500 (the 2027 limit hadn't been announced at the time of writing). Invested every year from 25 to 65 at a 7% average return, that grows to about $1.5 million.

What nobody tells you: Roth money goes in after tax, so qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax free. That includes all the growth.

Things to know before opening one:
• There are income limits for contributing directly
• Contributions (not earnings) can usually be withdrawn any time
• Earnings have rules: generally age 59½ and 5 years
• Returns aren't guaranteed, markets go up and down

Getting started:
1. Open a Roth IRA at a low-cost brokerage
2. Choose a broad index fund or target date fund
3. Set an automatic monthly contribution, even $50

Is a Roth IRA already open, or still on the to-do list?

#JustMoney #RothIRA #Investing

card:
Renting isn't throwing money away.

Paying 7% interest, property taxes, insurance, and a $10,000 roof isn't free either.

Run the numbers for the city before letting anyone shame either choice.
caption:
"Renting is throwing money away" might be the most repeated money advice out there. It's not that simple.

Owning has costs that never build equity:
• Mortgage interest (huge in the early years, with rates near 7%)
• Property taxes
• Homeowners insurance
• Repairs and maintenance (a roof can cost $10,000 or more)
• Closing costs when buying and selling

Renting has costs too, mainly rent going up and no equity.

What nobody tells you: in some cities renting and investing the difference beats buying. In others, buying wins. It depends on the numbers, not the slogan.

How to decide:
1. Use a rent vs buy calculator with real local numbers
2. Plan to stay at least 5 years before buying makes sense
3. Count maintenance at 1% to 2% of the home's value per year
4. Keep an emergency fund separate from the down payment

Both paths can build wealth. Both can go wrong.

Renting or owning right now, and how's it going?

#JustMoney #RentVsBuy #RealEstate

card:
Carrying a balance does NOT help the credit score.

Paying in full every month builds the same history without paying 20% for the privilege.
caption:
This myth costs people a lot of money: "Leave a small balance to build credit."

Nope.

Credit scores look at whether bills are paid on time and how much of the available credit is being used. Carrying a balance month to month doesn't earn extra points. It just earns interest.

What nobody tells you: the balance that shows on the statement is what usually gets reported. Paying in full after that still helps payment history without any interest.

What actually builds credit:
1. Pay every bill on time, every time (autopay helps)
2. Keep the reported balance low compared to the limit, under 30% is a common guideline
3. Keep old accounts open when possible
4. Only apply for new credit when needed
5. Check credit reports for free at annualcreditreport.com

Good credit and paying zero interest can happen at the same time.

Who else was told to "leave a little balance" growing up?

#JustMoney #CreditScore #CreditCards

card:
Lose the job on Friday. Rent is due on the 1st.

That's the whole reason to have 3 to 6 months of expenses saved.

Not a vibe. A plan.
caption:
Layoffs don't send a calendar invite.

The email shows up on a Friday. Rent is still due on the 1st. The car payment doesn't pause.

That's exactly what an emergency fund is for.

What nobody tells you: unemployment benefits can take weeks to start, and they usually replace only part of the paycheck.

How to build a cushion that actually works:
1. Add up only the must-pay bills: rent, utilities, food, insurance, minimum debt payments
2. Multiply by 3 for a starter goal, 6 for a stronger one
3. Keep it in a high-yield savings account, not checking
4. Automate a transfer every payday, any amount
5. Know the plan: which subscriptions get cut first

Job security isn't fully in anyone's control. Savings is.

How many months of bills could the savings account cover right now?

#JustMoney #EmergencyFund #Layoffs

card:
A $35,000 wedding is one day.

$35,000 invested at 30 could be about $265,000 by 60.
caption:
One day vs thirty years. Same $35,000.

This isn't about skipping a wedding. It's about knowing what the money could do.

$35,000 invested at age 30 with a 7% average annual return could grow to about $265,000 by age 60. That's just the math of compound growth, not a guarantee.

What nobody tells you: plenty of couples start married life with wedding debt. That's a rough way to begin.

Ways to have a great day without the long hangover:
• Cut the guest list, it drives almost every other cost
• Pick an off-peak day or season
• Skip what nobody will remember (chair covers, favors)
• Set the budget together BEFORE booking anything
• Pay cash, not credit

Spend on what matters to the two people getting married. Not what matters to the Pinterest board.

Would a smaller wedding and a bigger savings account be worth it?

#JustMoney #WeddingBudget #MoneyGoals

card:
In every state, daycare for two kids costs more than the average rent.

Two parents work full time to afford the daycare that lets both parents work full time.
caption:
For a lot of families, the second paycheck mostly goes to daycare.

Child Care Aware of America found that center-based care for two kids costs more than average rent in every state, and at least twice as much in 11 states plus D.C.

Average care costs were near $11,600 per child per year in that report. Some states run much higher.

What nobody tells you: there are tax breaks and benefits that can soften this, but many families never use them.

Places to look:
1. Dependent Care FSA through work (pre-tax money for childcare)
2. The Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit at tax time
3. State childcare assistance programs, check eligibility even if it seems unlikely
4. Employer childcare benefits or backup care
5. Shared care or nanny shares with another family

Childcare is one of the biggest bills a family will ever have. It deserves a real plan.

Is childcare the biggest monthly bill right now?

#JustMoney #Childcare #FamilyFinance

card:
Most professional large-cap fund managers trail the S&P 500 over 15 years.

A cheap index fund beats them by just showing up.
caption:
Paying for a professional stock picker doesn't usually win. The data is pretty clear.

S&P's SPIVA scorecard found that about 90% of actively managed U.S. large-cap funds trailed the S&P 500 over 15 years (through 2024).

What nobody tells you: fees are a big part of it. A 1% fee every year quietly eats a huge chunk of long-term growth.

Why index funds work for most people:
• They own the whole market, so no guessing
• Fees are often tiny, some under 0.05%
• They're simple enough to set and forget
• They don't need anyone to "beat" anything

Getting started:
1. Check the expense ratio on every fund in the 401(k)
2. Look for a broad US or total market index fund
3. Add a total international fund for diversification if desired
4. Keep investing through ups and downs

Boring investing tends to beat exciting investing.

What's the expense ratio on the funds in the 401(k)?

#JustMoney #IndexFunds #Investing

card:
A side hustle making $1,000 a month is great.

Just know self-employment tax is about 15.3% before income tax even shows up.

Set aside 25% to 30% so April isn't a surprise.
caption:
The side hustle money feels like a bonus. Until April.

When nobody withholds taxes from a paycheck, the taxes are still owed.

Self-employment tax is about 15.3% (Social Security and Medicare, both halves). Regular income tax comes on top of that.

On $12,000 a year of side income, that can add up fast.

What nobody tells you: business expenses can lower the taxable amount, but only if they're tracked.

How to stay ahead:
1. Move 25% to 30% of every payment into a separate savings account
2. Track expenses (software, mileage, supplies) all year
3. Look into quarterly estimated tax payments to avoid penalties
4. Keep receipts in one folder or app
5. Talk to a tax pro the first year, it often pays for itself

Earning extra is great. Keeping it is better.

What's the side hustle, and how's it going?

#JustMoney #SideHustle #Taxes

card:
Income is what you make. Net worth is what you keep.

Plenty of $150k earners have a lower net worth than a $55k earner who just doesn't finance everything.
caption:
A big salary and a big net worth are not the same thing.

Income is what comes in. Net worth is what's left: everything owned minus everything owed.

Someone making $150,000 with a huge mortgage, two car loans and credit card debt can have a smaller net worth than someone making $55,000 who lives below their means.

What nobody tells you: high earners often get offered more credit, which makes it easier to spend income before it ever becomes wealth.

How to track it in 10 minutes:
1. List all assets: savings, retirement, investments, home value
2. List all debts: mortgage, car loans, student loans, cards
3. Subtract debts from assets
4. Repeat every 3 to 6 months

The number might be negative at first. That's normal, especially with student loans. The direction matters more than the starting point.

Has anyone here actually calculated their net worth?

#JustMoney #NetWorth #PersonalFinance

card:
Save what's left after spending, and there's never anything left.

Spend what's left after saving, and there always is.
caption:
The order matters more than the amount.

Most people try to save whatever is left at the end of the month. There's rarely anything left. Spending expands to fill the space.

Flip it, and saving happens first. Spending adjusts to what remains.

What nobody tells you: this works because it removes willpower from the equation. The money is gone before there's a chance to spend it.

How to set it up:
1. Pick a starting number, even 5% of take-home pay
2. Schedule an automatic transfer for payday, not later in the month
3. Send it to a separate savings or investment account
4. Increase it by 1% every few months
5. Treat it like a bill that must be paid

Paying the future self first isn't selfish. It's the whole point.

What percent of the paycheck gets saved before anything else?

#JustMoney #PayYourselfFirst #Savings

card:
Most rental counters won't hand an 18-year-old the keys to a Corolla.

But that same 18-year-old can sign for $30,000 in student loans with no credit check.
caption:
Too young to rent a car at most counters. Old enough to sign for tens of thousands in debt.

Federal student loans for undergrads usually don't require a credit check. A dependent student can borrow up to $31,000 in federal loans over their undergrad years, and private loans can push it higher.

What nobody tells you: student loans are very hard to get rid of, even in bankruptcy.

Before signing:
1. Look at the expected salary for the major
2. Try to keep total borrowing below that first-year salary
3. Fill out the FAFSA every year, grants are free money
4. Consider community college for the first two years
5. Max out federal loans before private ones (more protections)

College can absolutely be worth it. It just deserves the same math as any other big purchase.

What do people wish they'd known about student loans at 18?

#JustMoney #StudentLoans #College

card:
Unpopular opinion: The safest job in 2026 is the one with 6 months of savings behind it.

Titles change. Departments get "restructured."

The savings account never gets a reorg email.
caption:
No job title is layoff proof. A savings account kind of is.

Restructuring, reorgs, "strategic realignment." It all means the same thing for the people affected.

What nobody tells you: the people who handle layoffs best usually aren't the ones with the fanciest roles. They're the ones with cash and a plan.

Building job security that belongs to the employee, not the employer:
• 3 to 6 months of must-pay expenses saved
• An updated resume, even when things feel fine
• A professional network that gets attention before it's needed
• Skills that work at more than one company
• Low fixed bills, so a smaller paycheck still works

Loyalty to an employer is fine. Just keep a backup plan too.

What's one thing that would make a surprise layoff less scary?

#JustMoney #JobSecurity #EmergencyFund

card:
A 4% raise on $50,000 is $2,000 a year.

After taxes, that's about $130 a month.

That's why the STARTING salary is the one to negotiate.
caption:
A "4% raise" sounds big. Then it hits the paycheck.

$2,000 a year more on a $50,000 salary. After federal tax, Social Security and Medicare, that's roughly $130 a month, a bit less with state tax.

What nobody tells you: future raises are usually a percentage of the current salary. A low starting number follows someone for years.

Why the starting salary matters most:
• Every future raise builds on it
• Retirement matches are a percentage of it
• The next employer often anchors to it

How to negotiate the offer:
1. Research the market range for the role and city
2. Let the employer name a number first when possible
3. Counter with a specific number, not a range
4. Negotiate the full package (PTO, sign-on bonus, remote days)
5. Get the final offer in writing

One uncomfortable conversation can be worth thousands every year.

Has anyone negotiated a first offer and gotten more?

#JustMoney #SalaryNegotiation #CareerTips

card:
The mortgage is just the cover charge.

Property taxes. Insurance. HOA. The water heater. The AC that dies in August.

Budget 1% to 2% of the home's value every year for repairs alone.
caption:
The mortgage payment is just the price of getting in the door.

Homeownership comes with a lot of costs that don't show up on the listing:
• Property taxes (and they can go up)
• Homeowners insurance (rising fast in many states)
• HOA fees
• Repairs that never ask permission

What nobody tells you: a common rule of thumb is to set aside 1% to 2% of the home's value every year for maintenance. On a $350,000 home, that's $3,500 to $7,000 a year.

How to avoid getting blindsided:
1. Ask for the last 2 years of tax and utility costs before buying
2. Get an inspection, and ask how old the roof, AC and water heater are
3. Open a separate "house fund" savings account
4. Shop homeowners insurance every year
5. Fix small problems before they become big ones

A house can be a great investment. It's also a very expensive hobby.

What was the most surprising house expense so far?

#JustMoney #Homeownership #Budgeting

card:
Car insurance went up again.

Same car. Same driver. Same zero accidents.

Shop it every year. Loyalty is the most expensive discount there is.
caption:
Clean record. Same car. And the bill went up anyway.

Car insurance prices have climbed a lot in recent years. Repairs cost more, cars are more expensive to replace, and those costs get passed on.

What nobody tells you: some insurers raise rates on long-time customers because they don't expect them to shop around. Staying put can cost money.

How to push the price down:
1. Get quotes from at least 3 companies every renewal
2. Ask about discounts: bundling, safe driver, low mileage, good student
3. Raise the deductible if the emergency fund can cover it
4. Drop collision coverage on older, low-value cars (do the math first)
5. Check the credit report, in many states it affects the rate

20 minutes of quotes can save hundreds a year.

When was the last time the car insurance got shopped around?

#JustMoney #CarInsurance #SaveMoney

card:
Social Security got a 3.6% raise for 2027.

That's about $75 more a month on average.

Rent, groceries, and Medicare premiums got the memo too.
caption:
A raise for retirees is coming in January. It might not feel like one.

The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027. For the average retired worker, that's about $75 more a month.

What nobody tells you: Medicare Part B premiums usually come out of the Social Security check, and those often rise too. So the take-home raise can be smaller than the headline.

What this means at any age:
• Social Security replaces only part of working income
• Inflation hits retirees hard because income is fixed
• Personal savings matter a lot for a comfortable retirement

Things to do now:
1. Create a free online account at ssa.gov to see estimated benefits
2. Check that earnings history is correct
3. Keep contributing to a 401(k) or IRA, even small amounts
4. For parents or grandparents, help them review the new benefit letter in December

Retirement planning isn't just for retirees.

Does anyone in the family rely on Social Security right now?

#JustMoney #SocialSecurity #Retirement

card:
2% cash back means nothing at 20% APR.

Rewards are for people who pay in full. For everyone else, they're bait.
caption:
Earning 2% while paying 20% isn't a strategy. It's a trap with a nice logo.

Rewards cards only "win" when the full balance is paid every month. Carry a balance and the interest wipes out the rewards many times over.

Quick math: $3,000 carried at 20% APR costs about $600 a year in interest. 2% cash back on $3,000 of spending is $60.

What nobody tells you: rewards cards often have higher APRs than simple cards. The points are paid for somehow.

How to use them the smart way:
1. Only use a rewards card if paying it off in full is a habit
2. Set up autopay for the full statement balance
3. Skip cards with annual fees unless the math clearly works
4. If carrying debt, switch focus to paying it down, not earning points

Points are a nice bonus. They're never worth the interest.

Is the credit card paid in full every month, or is that the goal?

#JustMoney #CreditCards #CashBack

card:
Two friends both make $70,000.

One drives a paid-off 2015 Camry and invests $787 a month.
The other has a $787 car payment.

In 10 years, one has about $136,000. The other has a used car.
caption:
Same salary. Same 10 years. Very different outcomes.

$787 a month is the average new car payment right now (Edmunds, Q3 2026).

Invested instead, $787 a month for 10 years at a 7% average return grows to about $136,000. That's not a guarantee, markets move. But it shows the trade.

Meanwhile, the car that cost $787 a month is worth a fraction of what was paid after a decade.

What nobody tells you: nobody needs to choose between a nice car and zero car. The middle option, a reliable used car, often wins.

How to make the switch:
1. Keep the paid-off car as long as it's safe and reliable
2. Keep "paying" the car payment, but to an investment account
3. Save for the next car in cash
4. Buy 2 to 3 years used when it's time to replace it

The car gets people places. The investments get them further.

Which friend is closer to the current plan?

#JustMoney #Investing #CarPayment

card:
December: "It's the holidays."

January: "Why is the credit card $2,400?"
caption:
The holidays are fun. The January statement is not.

Gifts, travel, parties, decorations, one more "just a little something." It all feels small in the moment and very large 30 days later.

What nobody tells you: holiday spending carried on a card at around 20% APR can still be costing money in July.

How to keep December from wrecking January:
1. Set one total holiday budget today, not a per-gift guess
2. Write the list of people and a number next to each name
3. Suggest a gift exchange or name draw for big groups
4. Pay with debit or cash, or pay the card weekly
5. Start a small "holiday fund" in January for next year

Generosity doesn't have to come with interest.

What's the holiday budget this year, or is there one yet?

#JustMoney #HolidayBudget #DebtFree

card:
Millions of homeowners locked in mortgages under 4%.

Rates are over 7%.

Nobody is moving. That's why there's nothing for sale.
caption:
Why are there so few homes for sale? A lot of it comes down to one number.

Millions of homeowners got mortgages under 4% during the low-rate years. Today's 30-year rate is above 7% (Freddie Mac, late October).

Selling would mean giving up a cheap loan for a much more expensive one. So many people stay put. Fewer listings means higher prices for buyers.

What nobody tells you: this "lock-in effect" can last for years, until life events like new jobs, kids and downsizing force moves.

For buyers right now:
1. Look at new construction, builders sometimes offer rate buydowns
2. Ask about assumable loans (some FHA and VA loans allow it)
3. Get pre-approved so offers move fast
4. Don't stretch the budget assuming rates will drop soon

For owners with low rates: that loan is a valuable asset. Moving should be a real decision, not an impulse.

Is the housing market where you live frozen too?

#JustMoney #HousingMarket #MortgageRates

card:
Nobody taught most people how a credit score works, what a Roth IRA is, or why the minimum payment is a trap.

Learning it at 30 still beats learning it at 50.
caption:
Most schools skipped the class everyone actually needed.

Credit scores, interest, retirement accounts, taxes. A lot of people learn this stuff by making expensive mistakes first.

That's not a personal failure. It's a gap in how money gets taught.

What nobody tells you: the basics aren't complicated. They just never got explained.

A starter list to learn this year:
1. How a credit score is calculated (payment history matters most)
2. The difference between a Roth IRA and a traditional IRA
3. How interest works on credit cards vs savings
4. What an index fund is and why fees matter
5. How a paycheck is taxed

Ten minutes a week is enough. One topic at a time.

Learning late still counts. Every year earlier helps more.

What money lesson should have been taught in school?

#JustMoney #FinancialLiteracy #MoneyTips
